'''''Doryphora sassafras''''', commonly known as '''sassafras''', '''yellow sassafras''', '''golden deal''' or '''golden sassafras''',<ref name="FoA">{{cite web |last1=Foreman |first1=Donald B. |last2=Whiffin |first2=Trevor J. |title=''Doryphora sassafras'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Doryphora%20sassafras |publisher=Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water: Canberra |access-date=14 May 2024}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the southern sassafras family [[Atherospermataceae]] and is [[endemic]] to eastern Australia. It is a shrub to tree with elliptic or egg-shaped leaves and contrasting white flowers which occur in autumn and winter.
[[File:Doryphora sassafras habit.jpg|thumb|Habit in the [[Australian National Botanic Gardens]]]]
[[File:Doryphora sassafras, leaf detail.jpg|thumb|Leaf]]

==Description==
''Doryphora sassafras'' is a shrub or tree that typically grows to {{cvt|2.5–36|m|ft|-1}}.<ref name="FoA" /><ref name=Floyd>{{cite book |author-link=Alexander Floyd |first=Alexander G. |last=Floyd |title=Australian Rainforests in New South Wales |publisher=Surrey Beatty & Sons |location=Chipping Norton, NSW |volume=1 |date=1990 |isbn=0-949324-31-0 |oclc=954236141}}</ref> Its leaves are arranged in opposite pairs,<ref name="Fairley">{{cite book |last1=Fairley |first1=A. |last2=Moore |first2=P. |title=Native Plants of the Sydney District: An Identification Guide |year=2000 |edition=2nd |publisher=Kangaroo Press |location=Kenthurst, NSW |isbn=0-7318-1031-7 |page=53}}</ref> elliptic to [[lanceolate]] or [[ovate (leaf)|ovate]], {{cvt|30–110|mm|1}} long and {{cvt|15–40|mm|1}} wide on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|3–6|mm|1}} long.<ref name="FoA" /> The edges of the leaves are shallowly to deeply toothed, glabrous and glossy, and both surfaces have a prominent midvein.<ref name="FoA" /> All parts of the tree have a spicy smell,<ref name="Les">{{cite book |last1=Robinson |first1=Les |title=Field Guide to the Native Plants of Sydney |date=1991 |publisher=Kangaroo Press |location=Kenthurst |isbn=0-86417-192-7 |pages=353–4 |oclc=26018462}}</ref> but should be treated with "some caution", since the plant contains the poisonous alkaloid [[doryphorine]].<ref name="Cribb">{{cite book |last1=Cribb |first1=Alan B. |last2=Cribb |first2=Joan W. |title=Wild Food in Australia |date=1974 |publisher=Fontana |location=Sydney |isbn=0-00-634436-4 |pages=174 |oclc=28991851}}</ref> Each individual leaf on a sassafras has a lifespan up to 12 years,<ref name="Lowman">{{cite journal |last1=Lowman |first1=Marguerite |title=Leaf Growth Dynamics and Herbivory in five species of Australian rain-forest canopy trees |journal=Journal of Ecology |date=1992 |volume=80 |issue=3 |pages=433–447 |doi=10.2307/2260689 |jstor=2260689 |bibcode=1992JEcol..80..433L }}</ref> and exceptionally to 19 years.<ref>{{cite book| last=Preston | first= Richard | date= 2007 | title= The Wild Trees | location= New York | publisher= Random House | pages= 53–54 }}</ref>

The flowers are white with 6 [[tepal]]s in 2 [[Whorl (botany)|whorls]] mostly {{cvt|7–13|mm|1}} long and {{cvt|2.5–4|mm|1}} wide, the [[Stamen|androecium]] with usually 4 whorls with 6 [[stamen]]s and 14 to 18 [[staminode]]s, and there are 8 to 12 [[Gynoecium#Carpels|carpels]]. Flowering occurs from May to October and the [[achene]]s are {{cvt|3.5–5|mm|1}} long and {{cvt|2–3|mm|2}} in diameter.<ref name="FoA" />

==Taxonomy==
''Doryphora sassafras'' was first described in 1837 by Austrian naturalist [[Stephan Endlicher]] in 1837 in his ''[[Iconographia generum plantarum]]''.<ref name="APNI">{{cite web |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/rest/instance/apni/505266 |title=''Doryphora sassafras'' |website=[[Australian Plant Name Index]] (APNI) |publisher=Centre for Plant Biodiversity Research, [[Australian Government]] |access-date=14 May 2024}}</ref><ref name="Endl.">{{cite book |last1=Endlicher |first1=Stephan |title=Iconographia generum plantarum |date=1837 |publisher=F. Beck |location=Vienna |page=X |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/130502#page/14/mode/1up |access-date=15 May 2024}}</ref> Its generic name is derived from the [[Ancient Greek]] ''dory-'' "spear" and ''pherein'' "to carry", and refers to the anthers in the flower, while its specific epithet is taken from its similar odour to the North American Laurel (''[[Sassafras albidum]]'').<ref name="Floyd09">{{cite book |last=Floyd |first=Alexander G. |author-link=Alexander Floyd |title=Rainforest Trees of Mainland Southeastern Australia |publisher=Terania Rainforest Publishing |location=Lismore, NSW |year=2009 |pages=87–88 |isbn=978-0-9589436-7-3 |oclc=244437135 }}</ref> It is a member of the small Southern Sasafrass family ([[Atherospermataceae]]) along with several other Australian and [[Patagonian]] rainforest trees  including southern sassafras (''[[Atherosperma moschatum]]'').

==Distribution and habitat==
The distribution is from [[Nambour, Queensland|Nambour]] in southern Queensland through eastern New South Wales to Wolumla Peak in Yurammie State Forest. It is found in temperate rainforest on basalt soils at higher elevations and sedimentary soils at lower elevations, commonly associated with coachwood (''[[Ceratopetalum apetalum]]'') and native crabapple (''[[Schizomeria ovata]]'').<ref name="Floyd09"/>

==Ecology==
Male mosquitoes and [[crane flies]] are attracted to the flowers of sassafras, but although they are [[nectarivore]]s, in their struggle to feed, they pollinate the flowers.<ref name="Les" />

==Uses==
===Timber===
The soft yellowish timber is used in floors, turnery, and cabinet work.<ref name="Floyd09"/>

===Use in horticulture===
It is used in reforestation but generally grows too big to be used in home gardens. It has been thought to have potential as a potted specimen.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Elliot | first1=Rodger W. | last2=Jones | first2=David L. | last3=Blake | first3=Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation |volume=3|year=1989 |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne |isbn=0-85091-167-2|page=331 |oclc=8298539}}</ref> It has been planted in [[Dublin]] area in [[Ireland]]<ref name="The Garden Flora of Northern Ireland" >{{cite web|url=http://www.earlscliffe.com/climatic_zone_plants.htm|title=Climatic zone plants|publisher=Earlscliffe|accessdate=2009-11-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721193555/http://www.earlscliffe.com/climatic_zone_plants.htm|archive-date=2011-07-21|url-status=dead}}</ref>
